To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

repeated immobilization stress results in a significant up-regulation of vasopressin expression and release in the hypothalamus, and that this effect is accompanied by a significant increase in CRF- and VP-containing neurons.
repeated stress increases CRF and VP expression in parvocellular paraventricular hypothalamic neurons and that this increase may lead to changes in the composition of ACTH-releasing factors.
repeated stress exposure leads to an increase in CRF and VP expression by hypophysiotrophic neurons and that these changes may be related to alterations in the ACTH-releas ing signal.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the regulation of CRF and its co-released partner, VP, in the paraventricular nucleus and their possible role in stress-induced ACTH hypersecretion.
the regulation of neurohormonal expression in the hypothalamic paraventricular nucleus
a detailed analysis of the neuroanatomical changes occurring in the hypothalamus-pituitary-adrenal axis after stress exposure.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the repeated exposure of rats (and probably humans) to stress induces changes in the expression and distribution of the CRF and VP systems that may be involved in the pathogenesis of stress-related disorders.

repeated stress induces a significant upregulation of VP and CRF in parvicellular neurons of the hypothalamic paraventricular nucleus and a concomitant increase in the number of CRF neurons that are VP positive.

repeated exposure to immobilization stress results in a significant increase (200% of controls) in the cellular level of VP mRNA in the paraventricular nucleus and a 100% increase in the number of VP-containing parvicellular neurons, as well as a 50% increase in the proportion and a 1000% increase in the intensity of VP labeling in the median eminence CRF nerve terminals.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
repeated stress exposure leads to increased CRF expression and increased CRF-VP coexpression in parvicellular neurons of the PVN.
repeated stress results in an increased number of VP neurons and an increased expression of both CRF and VP in the hypophysiotropic CRF neurons.
stress-induced changes in CRF and VP expression in the paraventricular nucleus may contribute to the long-term regulation of ACTH secretion.
The main takeaway from our work is that

repeated exposure of rats (and possibly other mammals) to immobilization stress leads to a substantial increase in the number of VP- and CRH-expressing neurons in the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus.
repeated stress induces a marked increase in the number of VP neurons in the paraventricular nucleus, and that the majority of CRF neurons in this nucleus are VP positive after repeated stress.

stress exposure leads to an increase in CRF expression in the paraventricular nucleus, which in turn leads to an increase of CRF in the median eminence, and this increase is accompanied by an increase in VP expression and content in the median eminences.
